claims.source: We further found that feeding mice an iron-reduced diet alleviates iron accumulation in RPMs, enhances their ability to clear erythrocytes, and reduces damage.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing improved erythrophagocytosis capacity in aged IR mice (Figure 1L).

claims.claim: An iron-reduced diet reduces damage to RPMs.
claims.source: We further found that feeding mice an iron-reduced diet alleviates iron accumulation in RPMs, enhances their ability to clear erythrocytes, and reduces damage.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and improved mitochondrial function in aged IR RPMs.

claims.claim: Dietary iron reduction ameliorates hemolysis of splenic RBCs in aging mice.
claims.source: Consequently, this diet ameliorates hemolysis of splenic RBCs and reduces the burden of protein aggregates, mildly increasing serum iron availability in aging mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced extracellular heme levels in aged IR spleens (Figure 2E).

claims.claim: Dietary iron reduction reduces the burden of protein aggregates in aging mice.
claims.source: Consequently, this diet ameliorates hemolysis of splenic RBCs and reduces the burden of protein aggregates, mildly increasing serum iron availability in aging mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological staining and measurements of iron and heme content in aggregates from aged IR mice (Figure 2K, L).

claims.claim: Dietary iron reduction mildly increases serum iron availability in aging mice.
claims.source: Consequently, this diet ameliorates hemolysis of splenic RBCs and reduces the burden of protein aggregates, mildly increasing serum iron availability in aging mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing partial alleviation of decreased transferrin saturation in aged IR mice (Figure 1C).

claims.claim: RPM collapse is an early hallmark of aging.
claims.source: Taken together, we identified RPM collapse as an early hallmark of aging and demonstrated that dietary iron reduction improves iron turnover efficacy.
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course data showing RPM dysfunction beginning at 4-5 months of age (Figure 4).

claims.claim: Dietary iron reduction improves iron turnover efficacy.
claims.source: Taken together, we identified RPM collapse as an early hallmark of aging and demonstrated that dietary iron reduction improves iron turnover efficacy.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence showing improved RPM function, reduced splenic iron deposits, and improved systemic iron parameters in aged IR mice.

claims.claim: 80% of circulating iron is utilized for hemoglobin synthesis during the daily generation of approximately 200 billion red blood cells.
claims.source: At the systemic level, 80% of circulating iron is utilized for hemoglobin synthesis during the daily generation of approximately 200 billion red blood cells (RBCs) (Muckenthaler et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claims.claim: The oxygen-carrying capacity of RBCs renders them sensitive to the progressive build-up of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that drive natural RBCs senescence.
claims.source: The oxygen-carrying capacity of RBCs renders them sensitive to the progressive build-up of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that drive natural RBCs senescence (Bratosin et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claims.claim: 90% of the body iron needs are met by internal iron recycling from aged RBCs.
claims.source: To reduce the risk of RBC breakdown in the blood vessels and because mammals evolved under limited dietary iron availability, 90% of the body iron needs are met by internal iron recycling from aged RBCs (Ganz, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claims.claim: Iron recycling from aged RBCs is accomplished predominantly by red pulp macrophages (RPMs) of the spleen.
claims.source: This task is accomplished predominantly by red pulp macrophages (RPMs) of the spleen, cells that engulf defective RBCs in the process called erythrophagocytosis (EP; Bian et al., 2016; Youssef et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claims.claim: Only a fraction of RPMs actively perform phagocytosis of intact senescent RBCs at a given moment.
claims.source: Recent findings imply that in parallel to phagocytosis of intact senescent RBCs, which is actively performed by a fraction of RPMs at a given moment (Akilesh et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2021; Youssef et al., 2018) part of the RBC-derived iron is recovered via hemolysis of RBCs within the splenic microenvironment and subsequent hemoglobin uptake (Klei et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claims.claim: Part of the RBC-derived iron is recovered via hemolysis of RBCs within the splenic microenvironment and subsequent hemoglobin uptake.
claims.source: Recent findings imply that in parallel to phagocytosis of intact senescent RBCs, which is actively performed by a fraction of RPMs at a given moment (Akilesh et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2021; Youssef et al., 2018) part of the RBC-derived iron is recovered via hemolysis of RBCs within the splenic microenvironment and subsequent hemoglobin uptake (Klei et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent literature.

claims.claim: The loss of elasticity due to a build-up of oxidative damage is a key feature of naturally aged RBCs.
claims.source: The loss of elasticity due to a build-up of oxidative damage is a key feature of naturally aged RBCs (Arashiki et al., 2013; Bratosin et al., 1998; Ganz, 2012; Higgins, 2015; Lutz, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claims.claim: The unique architecture of the spleen confers a filter for verifying the biomechanical integrity of RBCs, whereby senescent rigid RBCs are retained within the spleen cords.
claims.source: The unique architecture of the spleen confers a filter for verifying the biomechanical integrity of RBCs, whereby senescent rigid RBCs are retained within the spleen cords (Mebius and Kraal, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claims.claim: Recognition of 'trapped' RBCs by RPMs involves mechanisms such as the binding of exoplasmic phosphatidylserine or opsonizing antibodies.
claims.source: Recognition of 'trapped' RBCs by RPMs involves additional mechanisms, such as the binding of exoplasmic phosphatidylserine or opsonizing antibodies, that were proposed to act additively (Gottlieb et al., 2012; Slusarczyk and Mleczko-Sanecka, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claims.claim: Upon engulfment by RPMs, RBCs are degraded in phagolysosomes, and heme is released to the cytoplasm by HRG1.
claims.source: Upon engulfment by RPMs, RBCs are degraded in phagolysosomes, and heme is released to the cytoplasm by HRG1 (Klei et al., 2017; Pek et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claims.claim: Heme is catabolized by heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1) to carbon monoxide (CO), biliverdin, and ferrous iron that feeds the labile iron pool (LIP).
claims.source: Heme is subsequently catabolized by heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1; encoded by Hmox1) to carbon monoxide (CO), biliverdin, and ferrous iron that feeds the labile iron pool (LIP) (Kovtunovych et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claims.claim: Iron from the LIP is sequestered by the iron-storing protein ferritin, composed of H and L subunits.
claims.source: Iron from the LIP is sequestered by the iron-storing protein ferritin, composed of H and L subunits (Mleczko-Sanecka and Silvestri, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claims.claim: Iron efflux from RPMs occurs via ferroportin (FPN) to replenish the transferrin-bound iron pool in the plasma.
claims.source: Iron efflux from RPMs occurs via ferroportin (FPN) to replenish the transferrin-bound iron pool in the plasma (Muckenthaler et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claims.claim: Hepcidin mediates FPN degradation and/or occlusion, hence preventing iron release from RPMs.
claims.source: The process of iron release from RPMs is tightly regulated by hepcidin, a liver-derived hormone that mediates FPN degradation and/or occlusion, hence preventing iron release from RPMs (Aschemeyer et al., 2018; Nemeth et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claims.claim: The rate of RBC clearance is very high, reaching 2–3 million per second in humans.
claims.source: Similar to erythropoiesis, the rate of RBC clearance is very high, reaching 2–3 million per second in humans (Higgins, 2015), and is considered largely constitutive under physiological conditions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claims.claim: The intensity of erythrophagocytosis can be enhanced by proinflammatory conditions and pathogen components.
claims.source: Some reports showed that the intensity of EP can be enhanced by proinflammatory conditions and pathogen components (Bennett et al., 2019; Bian et al., 2016; Delaby et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claims.claim: Altered calcium signaling in RPMs due to overactivation or the loss of the PIEZO1 mechanoreceptor controls erythrophagocytosis efficiency.
claims.source: Recent work employing genetic mouse models showed that altered calcium signaling in RPMs due to overactivation or the loss of the PIEZO1 mechanoreceptor controls EP efficiency (Ma et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent literature.

claims.claim: Iron dyshomeostasis hallmarks physiological aging.
claims.source: Iron dyshomeostasis hallmarks physiological aging.
claims.evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Physiological aging is exemplified by progressive iron accumulation and iron-dependent oxidative damage in aging organs.
claims.source: This is exemplified by progressive iron accumulation and iron-dependent oxidative damage in aging organs (Arruda et al., 2013; Cook and Yu, 1998; Sukumaran et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claims.claim: Limited plasma iron availability is frequent in aged individuals and is a leading cause of anemia in the elderly.
claims.source: At the same time, limited plasma iron availability is frequent in aged individuals and is a leading cause of a condition referred to as anemia in the elderly (Girelli et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claims.claim: RPMs are derived from embryonic progenitor cells.
claims.source: RPMs are derived from embryonic progenitor cells (Yona et al., 2013), exhibit low self-renewal capacity (Hashimoto et al., 2013), and are only partially replenished by blood monocytes during aging (Liu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claims.claim: RPMs exhibit low self-renewal capacity.
claims.source: RPMs are derived from embryonic progenitor cells (Yona et al., 2013), exhibit low self-renewal capacity (Hashimoto et al., 2013), and are only partially replenished by blood monocytes during aging (Liu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claims.claim: RPMs are only partially replenished by blood monocytes during aging.
claims.source: RPMs are derived from embryonic progenitor cells (Yona et al., 2013), exhibit low self-renewal capacity (Hashimoto et al., 2013), and are only partially replenished by blood monocytes during aging (Liu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claims.claim: Aged mice showed tissue iron loading, with the spleen being most affected, followed by the liver and other organs such as muscles and the heart.
claims.source: As expected, aged mice showed tissue iron loading, with the spleen being most affected, followed by the liver and other organs such as muscles and the heart (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data measuring non-heme iron content in various tissues.

claims.claim: Aging mice exhibited decreased blood hemoglobin values.
claims.source: Aging mice exhibited decreased blood hemoglobin values, as previously shown (Peters et al., 2008), and a drop in transferrin saturation, a feature that thus far was observed mostly in elderly humans (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F; Girelli et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Aging mice exhibited a drop in transferrin saturation.
claims.source: Aging mice exhibited decreased blood hemoglobin values, as previously shown (Peters et al., 2008), and a drop in transferrin saturation, a feature that thus far was observed mostly in elderly humans (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F; Girelli et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to literature on elderly humans.

claims.claim: RPMs in aged mice exhibited a significant deficiency in H ferritin levels.
claims.source: Using intracellular staining and flow cytometric analyses, we uncovered that RPMs [gated as CD11b-dim, F4/80-high, TREML4-high (Haldar et al., 2014) as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2] in aged mice exhibited a significant deficiency in H ferritin levels, with unchanged L ferritin protein expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, H; see Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B for validation of antibodies for intracellular staining).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data with validated antibodies.

claims.claim: RPMs in aged mice showed unchanged L ferritin protein expression.
claims.source: Using intracellular staining and flow cytometric analyses, we uncovered that RPMs [gated as CD11b-dim, F4/80-high, TREML4-high (Haldar et al., 2014) as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2] in aged mice exhibited a significant deficiency in H ferritin levels, with unchanged L ferritin protein expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, H; see Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B for validation of antibodies for intracellular staining).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data with validated antibodies.

claims.claim: Aged RPMs exhibited a significant increase in labile iron pool (LIP).
claims.source: Consistently, using the fluorescent probe FerroOrange that interacts specifically with ferrous iron, we detected a significant increase in LIP in aged RPMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) accompanied by marked oxidative stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using the FerroOrange probe.

claims.claim: Aged RPMs exhibited marked oxidative stress.
claims.source: Consistently, using the fluorescent probe FerroOrange that interacts specifically with ferrous iron, we detected a significant increase in LIP in aged RPMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) accompanied by marked oxidative stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using CellROX Deep Red probe.

claims.claim: Aged RPMs showed a significant drop in RBC clearance capacity.
claims.source: Using this ex vivo approach, we detected a significant drop in RBC clearance capacity in aged compared to young RPMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ex vivo erythrophagocytosis assay data.

claims.claim: The capacity of aged RPMs for the engulfment of zymosan remained unchanged.
claims.source: Notably, their capacity for the engulfment of zymosan remained unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L), thus suggesting a specific defect of EP in aged RPMs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ex vivo phagocytosis assay data using zymosan particles.

claims.claim: Aged RPMs showed decreased lysosomal activity compared to young RPMs.
claims.source: Using a fluorescent probe, we observed decreased lysosomal activity in RPMs isolated from 10- to 11-month-old mice compared to those derived from young control animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1M).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using a lysosomal activity assay kit.

claims.claim: Aged RPMs showed diminished mitochondrial activity.
claims.source: Of note, we also detected diminished mitochondrial activity, a well-established aging marker (Sun et al., 2016), in aged RPMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1N).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using the TMRE probe and a citation to literature on aging markers.

claims.claim: Peritoneal macrophages of aged mice did not show altered ROS levels or impaired functions of lysosomes and mitochondria.
claims.source: Interestingly, peritoneal macrophages of aged mice did not show altered ROS levels or impaired functions of lysosomes and mitochondria (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), suggesting that these age-related changes affect RPMs earlier than other macrophage populations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data on peritoneal macrophages.

claims.claim: Age-related changes in ROS levels and lysosomal/mitochondrial function affect RPMs earlier than other macrophage populations.
claims.source: Interestingly, peritoneal macrophages of aged mice did not show altered ROS levels or impaired functions of lysosomes and mitochondria (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), suggesting that these age-related changes affect RPMs earlier than other macrophage populations.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of RPM and peritoneal macrophage data.

claims.claim: Caloric restriction was previously shown to effectively reduce tissue iron content in older rats.
claims.source: Caloric restriction was previously shown to effectively reduce tissue iron content in older rats (Cook and Yu, 1998; Xu et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: An iron-reduced diet (25 ppm) is sufficient to maintain erythropoiesis.
claims.source: Analogously, to correct iron dyshomeostasis in aging mice, we reduced dietary iron content from the fifth week of life to a level (25 ppm) that was reported as sufficient to maintain erythropoiesis (Sorbie and Valberg, 1974).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: An iron-reduced diet reverted the degree of iron deposition in the spleen and liver of aged mice.
claims.source: This approach reverted the degree of iron deposition in the spleen and liver (Figure 1A and B) and partially alleviated the decreased transferrin saturation characteristic of aged mice fed a standard diet (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data measuring non-heme iron content.

claims.claim: An iron-reduced diet partially alleviated the decreased transferrin saturation in aged mice.
claims.source: This approach reverted the degree of iron deposition in the spleen and liver (Figure 1A and B) and partially alleviated the decreased transferrin saturation characteristic of aged mice fed a standard diet (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data measuring transferrin saturation.

claims.claim: The mild drop in blood hemoglobin was not rescued by the iron-reduced diet.
claims.source: Notably, the mild drop in blood hemoglobin was not rescued by the iron-reduced (IR) diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data measuring blood hemoglobin.

claims.claim: Aged mice did not display significant changes in hematocrit, RBCs counts, MCV, MCH, or the intensity of bone marrow erythropoiesis.
claims.source: Of note, aged mice did not display significant changes in hematocrit, RBCs counts, MCV, MCH, or the intensity of bone marrow erythropoiesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B–F; see Figure 1—figure supplement 6 for gating strategy of erythroid progenitors).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from blood analysis and flow cytometry.

claims.claim: Aged mice showed a small increase in extramedullary erythropoietic activity in the spleen.
claims.source: We observed a small increase in extramedullary erythropoietic activity in the spleen and increased plasma erythropoietin (EPO) levels in aged mice, implying that very mild anemic phenotype and/or decreased transferrin saturation are sensed by the body (Figure 1—figure supplement 5G, H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data measuring erythroid progenitor cells in the spleen.

claims.claim: Aged mice showed increased plasma erythropoietin (EPO) levels.
claims.source: We observed a small increase in extramedullary erythropoietic activity in the spleen and increased plasma erythropoietin (EPO) levels in aged mice, implying that very mild anemic phenotype and/or decreased transferrin saturation are sensed by the body (Figure 1—figure supplement 5G, H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ELISA data measuring plasma EPO.

claims.claim: Hepcidin mRNA levels were increased in the liver of aged versus young mice.
claims.source: Next, we observed that hepcidin mRNA levels were increased in the liver of aged versus young mice, a phenotype that was reverted by feeding them an IR diet (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data measuring hepcidin mRNA.

claims.claim: An iron-reduced diet reverted the increase in hepcidin mRNA levels in aged mice.
claims.source: Next, we observed that hepcidin mRNA levels were increased in the liver of aged versus young mice, a phenotype that was reverted by feeding them an IR diet (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data measuring hepcidin mRNA.

claims.claim: Plasma IL-6 levels remained unchanged in aged mice.
claims.source: In addition, we did not observe a contribution of inflammatory cues to hepcidin regulation, as the plasma IL-6 levels remained unchanged (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ELISA data measuring plasma IL-6.

claims.claim: Cell membrane FPN levels in RPMs were decreased in aged mice.
claims.source: As expected from the pattern of hepcidin expression, cell membrane FPN levels in RPMs were decreased in aged mice and this was rescued by feeding them an IR diet (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using a validated FPN antibody.

claims.claim: An iron-reduced diet rescued the decrease in cell membrane FPN levels in aged RPMs.
claims.source: As expected from the pattern of hepcidin expression, cell membrane FPN levels in RPMs were decreased in aged mice and this was rescued by feeding them an IR diet (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using a validated FPN antibody.

claims.claim: Accumulation of both labile iron and total iron was completely reversed in RPMs of aged mice fed an IR diet as compared to a standard diet.
claims.source: We found that despite decreased ferritin H levels in aged mice, regardless of the dietary regimen (Figure 1G), accumulation of both labile iron (Figure 1H) and total iron (Figure 1I) was completely reversed in RPMs of aged mice fed an IR diet as compared to a standard diet.
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using FerroOrange and iron assay data.

claims.claim: Oxidative stress in aged RPMs was alleviated in response to dietary iron restriction.
claims.source: Likewise, we observed alleviation of oxidative stress in aged RPMs in response to a dietary iron restriction (Figure 1J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using CellROX Deep Red probe.

claims.claim: There is a lower representation of RPMs in the spleens of aged mice.
claims.source: First, we detected a lower representation of RPMs in the spleens of aged mice, a phenotype that was alleviated by limited dietary iron content (Figure 1K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data quantifying RPM percentages.

claims.claim: Limited dietary iron content alleviated the lower representation of RPMs in aged spleens.
claims.source: First, we detected a lower representation of RPMs in the spleens of aged mice, a phenotype that was alleviated by limited dietary iron content (Figure 1K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data quantifying RPM percentages.

claims.claim: RPMs derived from aged mice on an IR diet showed mildly increased levels of the proliferation marker Ki-67.
claims.source: Consistent with the pattern of their regulation, we found that RPMs derived from aged mice on an IR diet showed mildly increased levels of the proliferation marker Ki-67 (Figure 1—figure supplement 8B), a phenomenon that was previously reported to drive RPM niche replenishment after erythrophagocytosis-driven depletion (Youssef et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data measuring Ki-67 and a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The shortage of RPMs during aging is chiefly driven by the depletion of RPMs of embryonic origin.
claims.source: Next, by reanalysis of published data from Ms4a3-tdTomato reporter mice (Liu et al., 2019) (where macrophages of monocyte origin are fluorescently labeled) we demonstrated that the shortage of RPMs during aging is chiefly driven by the depletion of RPMs of embryonic origin, whereas the low rate of RPM replenishment from monocytes remained constant during aging (Figure 1—figure supplement 9A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by reanalysis of published data from a reporter mouse model.

claims.claim: The low rate of RPM replenishment from monocytes remained constant during aging.
claims.source: Next, by reanalysis of published data from Ms4a3-tdTomato reporter mice (Liu et al., 2019) (where macrophages of monocyte origin are fluorescently labeled) we demonstrated that the shortage of RPMs during aging is chiefly driven by the depletion of RPMs of embryonic origin, whereas the low rate of RPM replenishment from monocytes remained constant during aging (Figure 1—figure supplement 9A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by reanalysis of published data from a reporter mouse model.

claims.claim: The drop in RPM representation is not underlain by insufficient recruitment from monocytes or a concurrent increase in granulocyte representation.
claims.source: In line with this, we did not observe any robust change in the splenic population of monocytes or pre-RPMs (Lu et al., 2020) in our aged mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 9B, C), and we did not detect significant differences in the numbers of granulocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 9D). These data suggest that the drop in RPM representation is not underlain by insufficient recruitment from monocytes or a concurrent increase in granulocyte representation, but involves the demise of embryonically derived cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from flow cytometry data showing no changes in monocytes, pre-RPMs, or granulocytes.

claims.claim: The drop in RPM representation involves the demise of embryonically derived cells.
claims.source: In line with this, we did not observe any robust change in the splenic population of monocytes or pre-RPMs (Lu et al., 2020) in our aged mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 9B, C), and we did not detect significant differences in the numbers of granulocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 9D). These data suggest that the drop in RPM representation is not underlain by insufficient recruitment from monocytes or a concurrent increase in granulocyte representation, but involves the demise of embryonically derived cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combination of data showing depletion of embryonic RPMs and no changes in monocyte recruitment.

claims.claim: Iron accumulation in RPMs, independently of ROS generation, is a major driver of erythrophagocytosis suppression during aging.
claims.source: Among them, iron accumulation in RPMs, independently of ROS generation, emerged as a major driver of EP suppression during aging, likely via the downregulation of apoptotic cell receptors (Slusarczyk and Mleczko-Sanecka, 2021) and calcium signaling (Ma et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that NAC treatment did not rescue EP defects, while iron reduction did, and by data showing downregulation of apoptotic cell receptors and calcium levels upon iron loading.

claims.claim: Aged RPMs were less efficient in sequestering transfused RBCs.
claims.source: We observed that aged RPMs were less efficient in sequestering transfused RBCs, an impairment that was partially rescued by feeding mice an IR diet (Figure 1L).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo erythrophagocytosis assay data.

claims.claim: Feeding mice an IR diet partially rescued the impairment in RBC sequestration by aged RPMs.
claims.source: We observed that aged RPMs were less efficient in sequestering transfused RBCs, an impairment that was partially rescued by feeding mice an IR diet (Figure 1L).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo erythrophagocytosis assay data.

claims.claim: RPMs isolated from aged IR mice restored lysosomal activity to the levels observed in young mice.
claims.source: Similarly to the EP rate, we found that RPMs isolated from aged IR mice restored the lysosomal activity to the levels observed in young mice (Figure 1M).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using a lysosomal activity assay.

claims.claim: Under conditions of RPM impairment, iron-recycling functions are significantly supported by liver macrophages.
claims.source: Since earlier studies demonstrated that under conditions of RPM impairment, iron-recycling functions are significantly supported by liver macrophages (Theurl et al., 2016), we also measured their EP capacity during aging.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in the percentage of RBC-positive hepatic macrophages in aged mice.
claims.source: Using the transfusion of PKH67-stained RBCs we did not detect significant differences in the percentage of RBC-positive hepatic macrophages in aged mice (Figure 1N).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from in vivo erythrophagocytosis assays.

claims.claim: There was a significant expansion of the KC-like population in aged mice but not in the aged IR group.
claims.source: However, consistently with the de novo recruitment of iron-recycling myeloid cells to the liver upon erythrocytic stress (Theurl et al., 2016), we noticed a significant expansion of the KC-like population in aged mice but not in the aged IR group (Figure 1O).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data quantifying KC populations and a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Liver macrophages may partially compensate for the decreased erythrophagocytosis activity in RPMs.
claims.source: This implies that the liver macrophage may partially compensate for the decreased EP activity in RPMs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the expansion of KC-like cells in aged mice with RPM dysfunction.

claims.claim: There were no differences in the rate of RBCs removal from the circulation between young and aged mice.
claims.source: First, we performed an RBC lifespan assay and found no differences in the rate of RBCs removal from the circulation between young and aged mice (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for RBC gating strategy), suggesting intact fitness of circulating RBCs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RBC biotinylation lifespan assay data.

claims.claim: Circulating RBCs from aged mice did not show increased labile iron or ROS levels.
claims.source: Likewise, these RBCs did not show increased labile iron or ROS levels (Figure 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using FerroOrange and CellROX probes.

claims.claim: RBCs isolated from the spleen of young mice showed ROS build-up, a marker of their natural senescence.
claims.source: In agreement with this model, RBCs isolated from the spleen of young mice showed ROS build-up, a marker of their natural senescence (Bratosin et al., 1998; Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data and a citation to literature on RBC senescence.

claims.claim: Splenic RBCs isolated from aged mice showed more pronounced ROS levels than RBCs derived from young mice.
claims.source: Consistently, splenic RBCs isolated from aged mice showed more pronounced ROS levels than RBCs derived from young mice (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using CellROX probe.

claims.claim: Mice fed an IR diet exhibited erythrocytic oxidative stress parameters similar to young mice.
claims.source: In line with the partial mitigation of the defective iron-recycling capacity by restricted dietary iron content (Figure 1K and L), we found that mice fed an IR diet exhibited erythrocytic oxidative stress parameters similar to the young mice (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data measuring ROS in splenic RBCs.

claims.claim: Significantly higher levels of extracellular heme were detected in aged spleens.
claims.source: In agreement with the notion that a part of senescent RBCs undergoes local hemolysis (Klei et al., 2020), we further detected significantly higher levels of extracellular heme in the aged spleens, likely reflecting a higher burden of defective RBCs that evade efficient EP (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by heme assay data and a citation to literature on splenic hemolysis.

claims.claim: The levels of heme in aging spleens were partially rescued by the IR diet.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that the levels of heme in aging spleens were partially rescued by the IR diet.
claims.evidence: This is supported by heme assay data comparing aged and aged IR mice.

claims.claim: Higher levels of heme were detected in plasma obtained from the portal vein of aged versus young mice.
claims.source: In support of these data, we detected higher levels of heme in plasma obtained from the portal vein (that carries the blood from the spleen to the liver) of aged versus young mice (Figure 2F) and higher serum concentrations of heme-scavenging hemopexin (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by heme assay data from portal vein plasma.

claims.claim: Higher serum concentrations of heme-scavenging hemopexin were detected in aged mice.
claims.source: In support of these data, we detected higher levels of heme in plasma obtained from the portal vein (that carries the blood from the spleen to the liver) of aged versus young mice (Figure 2F) and higher serum concentrations of heme-scavenging hemopexin (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ELISA data measuring serum hemopexin.

claims.claim: The reduced iron-recycling capacity of RPMs during aging may promote the retention of senescent RBCs prone to undergo local lysis.
claims.source: In conclusion, our data suggest that the reduced iron-recycling capacity of RPMs during aging may promote the retention of senescent RBCs prone to undergo local lysis and that these manifestations may be partially rescued by maintaining mice on an IR diet.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combination of data showing reduced EP capacity, increased splenic RBC ROS, and increased extracellular heme.

claims.claim: Genetic mouse models hallmarked by RPM depletion display splenic iron accumulation.
claims.source: Previous work showed that genetic mouse models hallmarked by RPM depletion display splenic iron accumulation (Haldar et al., 2014; Okreglicka et al., 2021), partially resembling our observation in aged mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Aged mice on a standard diet exhibited enhanced iron accumulation in the red pulp.
claims.source: Perls' Prussian blue staining that detects iron deposits showed that aged mice on a standard diet exhibited enhanced iron accumulation in the red pulp, a less pronounced phenotype in mice fed an IR diet (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological staining data.

claims.claim: Eosin and hematoxylin staining visualized deposits in aged spleens that were completely absent in young controls.
claims.source: Intriguingly, eosin and hematoxylin staining visualized deposits in aged spleens that, in contrast to Perls' staining, were completely absent in young controls (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological staining data.

claims.claim: Deposits in aged spleens appeared as large and extracellular in histology sections.
claims.source: They appeared as large and extracellular in the histology sections and seemed smaller and less abundant in mice fed an IR diet (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of histological images.

claims.claim: Splenic single-cell suspension from aged but not young mice contained superparamagnetic particles, likely rich in iron oxide.
claims.source: Flow cytometry analyses confirmed that splenic single-cell suspension from aged but not young mice contained superparamagnetic particles, likely rich in iron oxide (Franken et al., 2015), that are characterized by high granularity as indicated by the SSC-A signal (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data and a citation to literature on superparamagnetic particles.

claims.claim: Superparamagnetic particles in aged spleens did not show staining indicative of dead cells and failed to express typical splenocyte and erythroid markers.
claims.source: These particles did not show staining indicative of dead cells and failed to express typical splenocyte and erythroid markers (CD45, TER119, CD11b, or F4/80) (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data.

claims.claim: Magnetically isolated aggregates from aged spleens contained large amounts of total iron.
claims.source: We found that these aggregates contained large amounts of total iron (Figure 2K) and, interestingly, heme (Figure 2L), implying their partial RBC origin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by iron assay data on magnetically isolated aggregates.

claims.claim: Magnetically isolated aggregates from aged spleens contained heme.
claims.source: We found that these aggregates contained large amounts of total iron (Figure 2K) and, interestingly, heme (Figure 2L), implying their partial RBC origin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by heme assay data on magnetically isolated aggregates.

claims.claim: Both iron and heme content in splenic aggregates was significantly reduced in mice fed an IR diet.
claims.source: Importantly, both iron and heme content was significantly reduced in mice fed an IR diet.
claims.evidence: This is supported by iron and heme assay data comparing aged and aged IR aggregates.

claims.claim: RPMs in young mice contained only intracellular dark-colored deposits, rich in structures that resemble ferritin.
claims.source: We noticed that RPMs in young mice contained only intracellular dark-colored deposits, rich in structures that resemble ferritin (Figure 3Ai).
claims.evidence: This is based on TEM imaging observations.

claims.claim: In older mice, intracellular deposits were observed in morphologically intact cells.
claims.source: In older mice, we likewise observed intracellular deposits in morphologically intact cells (Figure 3Aii).
claims.evidence: This is based on TEM imaging observations.

claims.claim: In aged mice, aggregates that are granular and enclosed within the membrane were present in cells that are morphologically damaged.
claims.source: However, in agreement with histological staining, we detected two other classes of aggregates: those that are still granular and enclosed within the membrane, but present in cells that are morphologically damaged (Figure 3Aiii) and those that are large, amorphic, and located extracellularly (Figure 3Aiv).
claims.evidence: This is based on TEM imaging observations.

claims.claim: In aged mice, aggregates that are large, amorphic, and located extracellularly were detected.
claims.source: However, in agreement with histological staining, we detected two other classes of aggregates: those that are still granular and enclosed within the membrane, but present in cells that are morphologically damaged (Figure 3Aiii) and those that are large, amorphic, and located extracellularly (Figure 3Aiv).
claims.evidence: This is based on TEM imaging observations.

claims.claim: 3290 protein groups were significantly more abundant in isolates from aged mice compared with samples derived from young mice.
claims.source: We identified over 3770 protein groups, among which 3290 were significantly more abundant in isolates from aged mice compared with the samples derived from young mice (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by label-free quantification proteomic data.

claims.claim: One of the top characteristics shared by proteins in aging-triggered aggregates is a disordered region in their amino acid sequence.
claims.source: We first noticed that although the identified proteins were derived from different organelles, one of the top characteristics that they shared was a disordered region in their amino acid sequence, a factor that may increase the risk of protein aggregation (Uversky, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is based on functional enrichment analysis of proteomic data and a citation to literature on protein aggregation.

claims.claim: The top hits in aging-triggered aggregates were enriched in proteins related to neurodegeneration pathways.
claims.source: Consistently, the top hits were enriched in proteins related to neurodegeneration pathways, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, and heat shock protein binding, linking their origin to proteostasis defects (Medinas et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on functional enrichment analysis of proteomic data and a citation to literature on proteostasis.

claims.claim: Aging-triggered aggregates included aggregation-prone huntingtin (HTT), amyloid-beta precursor protein (APP), and ataxin 3 (ATXN3).
claims.source: These included aggregation-prone huntingtin (HTT), amyloid-beta precursor protein (APP), and ataxin 3 (ATXN3) (Lieberman et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2018 #251; Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on proteomic identification and citations to literature on aggregation-prone proteins.

claims.claim: 'Metal-binding' was identified as a significant functional enrichment in aging-triggered aggregates.
claims.source: In agreement with the substantial iron load of the aggregates and the fact that iron promotes protein aggregation (Klang et al., 2014), we identified 'metal-binding' as another significant functional enrichment.
claims.evidence: This is based on functional enrichment analysis and a citation to literature on iron-promoted aggregation.

claims.claim: The top components of aging-triggered aggregates included several proteins associated with immunoglobulin-like domains.
claims.source: We further observed that the top components of the aggregates included several proteins associated with immunoglobulin-like domains (Figure 3B and C), such as antibody chain fragments as well as Fc receptors, proteins associated with complement activation and phagocytosis, thus linking the aggregates to the removal of defective cells, likely senescent RBCs or damaged RPMs.
claims.evidence: This is based on proteomic identification and functional enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: The top components of aging-triggered aggregates were enriched with apoptosis-related proteins.
claims.source: Finally, consistent with our conclusions from EM imaging that cell death likely contributes to the formation of the aggregates (Figure 3Aiv), their top components were enriched with apoptosis-related protein (e.g. BID, DFFA, DAXX, and MRCH1; Figure 3B) and those linked to the response to stress (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: This is based on proteomic identification and functional enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: There is an overlap between protein components of aging-triggered aggregates and the proteome of RPMs and erythrocytes.
claims.source: Supporting the idea that iron-rich protein aggregates emerge primarily from damaged RPMs, and may likely contain some erythrocyte components, we observed an overlap between their protein components and the proteome of RPMs and erythrocytes (Gautier et al., 2018; Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of proteomic datasets and a citation to literature on erythrocyte proteome.

claims.claim: 570 differentially expressed genes were identified in aged versus young RPMs, including 392 up- and 178 down-regulated transcripts.
claims.source: We identified 570 differentially expressed genes, including 392 up- and 178 down-regulated transcripts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: RNA-seq data revealed an anti-inflammatory transcriptional pattern of aged RPMs.
claims.source: RNA-seq data revealed rather an anti-inflammatory transcriptional pattern of aged RPMs, exemplified by the downregulation of genes encoding for MHC class II complexes and the induction of Il10 (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Aged RPMs were hallmarked by ER stress, unfolded protein response, and ER-associated degradation (ERAD).
claims.source: Most importantly, functional enrichment analysis showed that aged RPMs were hallmarked by ER stress, unfolded protein response, and ER-associated degradation (ERAD) (Figure 3E), regardless of the diet (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on functional enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: There was a significant increase in proteasomal activity in aged RPMs.
claims.source: Correspondingly, we identified a significant increase in proteasomal activity in aged RPMs, measured with a dedicated fluorescent probe that undergoes proteasomal cleavage (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using a proteasome activity probe.

claims.claim: The IR diet reversed proteasomal activation in aged RPMs.
claims.source: The IR diet reversed this proteasomal activation (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data comparing aged and aged IR RPMs.

claims.claim: Forced iron accumulation in RPMs in response to iron dextran injection in young mice provoked the formation of iron-rich protein aggregates.
claims.source: Finally, assigning a causal relationship between the iron loading of RPMs and their global proteostasis defect, we found that forced iron accumulation in RPMs in response to iron dextran injection in young mice (Figure 3G) provoked the formation of iron-rich protein aggregates whose composition largely overlaps with those from aged spleens (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by iron assay and proteomic data from iron dextran-injected mice.

claims.claim: The composition of iron-rich protein aggregates formed after iron dextran injection largely overlaps with those from aged spleens.
claims.source: Finally, assigning a causal relationship between the iron loading of RPMs and their global proteostasis defect, we found that forced iron accumulation in RPMs in response to iron dextran injection in young mice (Figure 3G) provoked the formation of iron-rich protein aggregates whose composition largely overlaps with those from aged spleens (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomic comparison of aggregates from aged and iron dextran-injected mice.

claims.claim: Components of lysosomes were the most overrepresented hits in aggregates from aged mice compared to mice fed an IR diet.
claims.source: Functional enrichment analysis identified components of lysosomes as by far the most overrepresented hits (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B), suggesting that alleviation of the lysosomal defects likely contributes to less pronounced aggregates formation in iron-reduced mice.
claims.evidence: This is based on TMT-based proteomic quantification and functional enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Both H and L ferritin were significantly increased in aggregates from aged mice on a standard diet compared to an IR diet.
claims.source: The hits included also both H and L ferritin as being significantly increased in aggregates from aged mice on a standard diet.
claims.evidence: This is based on TMT-based proteomic quantification.

claims.claim: Cytoplasmic ferritin deficiency in aged RPMs may result from ferritin aggregation.
claims.source: Of note, we failed to detect ferritin in the aggregates using antibody staining and flow cytometry, thus suggesting that cytoplasmic ferritin deficiency (Figure 1G) may result from ferritin aggregation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combination of proteomic detection of ferritin in aggregates and flow cytometry showing decreased cytoplasmic ferritin.

claims.claim: RPMs started to show increased LIP levels early during age progression (at 5 months).
claims.source: We found that RPMs started to show increased LIP levels, and reduced their EP and lysosomal degradation capacity early during age progression (Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course flow cytometry data.

claims.claim: RPMs reduced their erythrophagocytosis capacity early during age progression (at 5 months).
claims.source: We found that RPMs started to show increased LIP levels, and reduced their EP and lysosomal degradation capacity early during age progression (Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course flow cytometry data.

claims.claim: RPMs reduced their lysosomal degradation capacity early during age progression (at 5 months).
claims.source: We found that RPMs started to show increased LIP levels, and reduced their EP and lysosomal degradation capacity early during age progression (Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course flow cytometry data.

claims.claim: At 5 months of age, a larger proportion of splenic RBCs exhibited increased ROS levels.
claims.source: Likewise, at 5 months of age, we observed that a larger proportion of splenic RBCs exhibited the senescence marker - increased ROS levels (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course flow cytometry data.

claims.claim: The accumulation of non-heme iron in the spleen occurred early during age progression.
claims.source: Interestingly, these changes reflected the accumulation of non-heme iron in the spleen and the appearance of splenic protein aggregates (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course iron assay and histological data.

claims.claim: The appearance of splenic protein aggregates occurred early during age progression.
claims.source: Interestingly, these changes reflected the accumulation of non-heme iron in the spleen and the appearance of splenic protein aggregates (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course histological data.

claims.claim: The drop in transferrin saturation during aging coincided with RPM failure and the appearance of splenic aggregates.
claims.source: In support of this possibility, we noticed that the drop in transferrin saturation during aging coincided with RPM failure and the appearance of splenic aggregates (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is based on time-course data showing parallel changes in these parameters.

claims.claim: Ferroportin dropped significantly already in mice aged 4 months.
claims.source: We observed that ferroportin dropped significantly already in mice aged 4 months, which at least partially was coupled with increased hepatic hepcidin expression (Figure 4H, I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course flow cytometry and qPCR data.

claims.claim: The drop in ferroportin at 4 months was at least partially coupled with increased hepatic hepcidin expression.
claims.source: We observed that ferroportin dropped significantly already in mice aged 4 months, which at least partially was coupled with increased hepatic hepcidin expression (Figure 4H, I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course flow cytometry and qPCR data.

claims.claim: At 4 months, RPMs started to exhibit decreased erythrophagocytosis activity.
claims.source: At the same time point, the cells started to exhibit decreased EP activity [here determined by intracellular staining of the erythrocytic marker TER119 in RPMs Akilesh et al., 2019; Figure 4J], and only afterward, at the age of 5 months, we detected significant retention of senescent, ROS-rich RBCs in the spleen (Figure 4K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course flow cytometry data and a citation to the method.

claims.claim: At 5 months, significant retention of senescent, ROS-rich RBCs in the spleen was detected.
claims.source: At the same time point, the cells started to exhibit decreased EP activity [here determined by intracellular staining of the erythrocytic marker TER119 in RPMs Akilesh et al., 2019; Figure 4J], and only afterward, at the age of 5 months, we detected significant retention of senescent, ROS-rich RBCs in the spleen (Figure 4K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course flow cytometry data.

claims.claim: Iron-triggered dysfunction of RPMs is initiated early during aging, likely due to ferroportin downregulation.
claims.source: In sum, our data show that iron-triggered dysfunction of RPMs is initiated early during aging, likely due to ferroportin downregulation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the time-course data showing early ferroportin decrease followed by RPM dysfunction.

claims.claim: Increased iron burden in RPMs was shown previously to drive ferroptotic cell death upon acute transfusion of damaged RBCs.
claims.source: Increased iron burden in RPMs was shown previously to drive ferroptotic cell death upon acute transfusion of damaged RBCs (Youssef et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Both labile iron and lipid peroxidation increased in RPMs during aging.
claims.source: In agreement with this hypothesis, both labile iron (Figure 4A), a factor that promotes ferroptosis, and lipid peroxidation (Figure 5A), a ferroptosis marker (Dixon et al., 2012; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014) increased in RPMs during aging.
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course flow cytometry data and citations to literature on ferroptosis markers.

claims.claim: Feeding mice an IR diet during aging diminished lipid peroxidation to the levels characteristic of young mice.
claims.source: Importantly, we observed that feeding mice an IR diet during aging diminished lipid peroxidation to the levels characteristic of young mice (Figure 5B), similar to what we observed for the labile iron build-up (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data comparing young, aged, and aged IR RPMs.

claims.claim: Injection of iron dextran in young mice led to robust lipid peroxidation in RPMs.
claims.source: In line with these findings, we observed that injection of iron dextran in young mice led to robust lipid peroxidation in RPMs (Figure 5C) and their mild depletion (p=0.056; Figure 5D) at 8 hr post-injection, before the formation of splenic protein aggregates occurred (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from iron dextran-injected mice.

claims.claim: Injection of iron dextran in young mice led to mild depletion of RPMs at 8 hr post-injection.
claims.source: In line with these findings, we observed that injection of iron dextran in young mice led to robust lipid peroxidation in RPMs (Figure 5C) and their mild depletion (p=0.056; Figure 5D) at 8 hr post-injection, before the formation of splenic protein aggregates occurred (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from iron dextran-injected mice.

claims.claim: Ferroptotic cells are characterized by reduced mitochondria size and diminished mitochondrial membrane potential but not mitochondrial oxidative stress.
claims.source: Earlier studies reported that ferroptotic cells are characterized by reduced mitochondria size and diminished mitochondrial membrane potential but not mitochondrial oxidative stress (Chen et al., 2021; Dixon et al., 2012; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014; Neitemeier et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on ferroptosis characteristics.

claims.claim: Aged RPMs failed to show augmented ROS levels in the mitochondria.
claims.source: Consistent with these data, we failed to detect augmented ROS levels in the mitochondria of aged RPMs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using MitoSOX probe.

claims.claim: Mitochondria mass decreased in RPMs of aged mice.
claims.source: Instead, we observed that mitochondria mass (Figure 5E), as well as mitochondrial activity (Figure 5F), decreased in RPMs of aged mice, and both these phenotypes were alleviated by an IR diet.
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using MitoTracker Green.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial activity decreased in RPMs of aged mice.
claims.source: Instead, we observed that mitochondria mass (Figure 5E), as well as mitochondrial activity (Figure 5F), decreased in RPMs of aged mice, and both these phenotypes were alleviated by an IR diet.
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using TMRE probe.

claims.claim: An IR diet alleviated the decrease in mitochondria mass and mitochondrial activity in aged RPMs.
claims.source: Instead, we observed that mitochondria mass (Figure 5E), as well as mitochondrial activity (Figure 5F), decreased in RPMs of aged mice, and both these phenotypes were alleviated by an IR diet.
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data comparing aged and aged IR RPMs.

claims.claim: Higher ATP levels were observed in FACS-sorted RPMs derived from aged mice fed an IR diet versus a standard diet.
claims.source: This corresponded to higher ATP levels in FACS-sorted RPMs derived from aged mice fed an IR diet versus a standard diet (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ATP assay data on sorted RPMs.

claims.claim: Mitochondria of ferroptotic cells are hallmarked by reduced size and fewer cristae, increased membrane density, and some appear swollen.
claims.source: Previous ultrastructural studies showed that mitochondria of ferroptotic cells are hallmarked by reduced size and fewer cristae, increased membrane density, and some appear swollen (Chen et al., 2021; Dixon et al., 2012; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on ferroptosis ultrastructure.

claims.claim: RPMs from aged animals exhibited mitochondrial defects including reduced size, fewer cristae, increased membrane density, and some appearing disintegrated.
claims.source: Consistently, our TEM imaging showed that in contrast to the RPMs of young mice, those from aged animals exhibited the above mitochondrial defects with some appearing disintegrated (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is based on TEM imaging observations.

claims.claim: Mitochondria from aged IR mice were small and dense, but displayed a lesser degree of swelling and damage.
claims.source: Mitochondria from mice fed an IR diet were small and dense, but they displayed a lesser degree of swelling and damage.
claims.evidence: This is based on TEM imaging observations.

claims.claim: Iron loading and blockage of ferroportin caused protein aggregation in iRPMs and led to their decreased viability only in cells exposed to heat shock.
claims.source: We observed that iron loading (with ferric ammonium citrate [FAC]) and blockage of ferroportin by synthetic mini-hepcidin (PR73) (Stefanova et al., 2018) caused protein aggregation in iRPMs and led to their decreased viability but only in cells that were exposed to heat shock, a well-established trigger of proteotoxicity (Figure 5H, I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro experiments with iRPMs and a citation to the mini-hepcidin reference.

claims.claim: FAC treatment increased lipid peroxidation to a similar extent in intact iRPMs and those exposed to heat shock.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed that although FAC treatment increased lipid peroxidation to a similar extent in intact cells and those exposed to heat shock (Figure 5J), cell viability was only reduced when the iron loading and proteotoxic challenge were combined (Figure 5K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro experiments.

claims.claim: Cell viability of iRPMs was only reduced when iron loading and proteotoxic challenge were combined.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed that although FAC treatment increased lipid peroxidation to a similar extent in intact cells and those exposed to heat shock (Figure 5J), cell viability was only reduced when the iron loading and proteotoxic challenge were combined (Figure 5K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro experiments.

claims.claim: The synergistic cytotoxic effect of iron loading and proteotoxic challenge was prevented by the ferroptosis blocker Liproxstatin-1.
claims.source: Even more strikingly, the latter synergistic cytotoxic effect was prevented by the ferroptosis blocker Liproxstatin-1 (Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014; Figure 5K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro experiments and a citation to the Liproxstatin-1 reference.

claims.claim: DNA fragmentation was detected in the spleens of aged mice.
claims.source: Finally, consistent with the observation that apoptosis markers can be elevated in tissues upon ferroptosis induction (Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014) and proteotoxicity may lead to apoptosis (Brancolini and Iuliano, 2020), we detected DNA fragmentation (via TUNEL assay) in the spleens of aged mice, a phenotype that was less pronounced in mice on an IR diet (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data and citations to literature on ferroptosis and proteotoxicity.

claims.claim: DNA fragmentation in aged spleens was less pronounced in mice on an IR diet.
claims.source: Finally, consistent with the observation that apoptosis markers can be elevated in tissues upon ferroptosis induction (Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014) and proteotoxicity may lead to apoptosis (Brancolini and Iuliano, 2020), we detected DNA fragmentation (via TUNEL assay) in the spleens of aged mice, a phenotype that was less pronounced in mice on an IR diet (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data.

claims.claim: RPM demise during aging is driven by iron-dependent cell death with ferroptosis characteristics coupled with proteostasis collapse.
claims.source: Taken together, our data suggest that RPM demise during aging is driven by iron-dependent cell death with ferroptosis characteristics coupled with proteostasis collapse.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combination of data showing lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial defects, ER stress, protein aggregation, and rescue by ferroptosis inhibitors.

claims.claim: NAC supplementation successfully reduced oxidative stress in aged RPMs.
claims.source: With this strategy, we successfully reduced oxidative stress in aged RPMs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from NAC-treated mice.

claims.claim: NAC supplementation did not improve the erythrophagocytosis capacity of RPMs isolated from aged mice.
claims.source: However, we did not observe an improvement in the EP capacity of RPMs isolated from NAC-supplemented mice compared to untreated aged mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from in vivo erythrophagocytosis assays.

claims.claim: NAC administration did not rescue the retention of senescent RBCs in the spleen.
claims.source: Consistently, the retention of senescent RBCs in the spleen (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) and their local hemolysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) were not rescued by the NAC administration.
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and heme assay data from NAC-treated mice.

claims.claim: NAC administration did not rescue local hemolysis of RBCs in the spleen.
claims.source: Consistently, the retention of senescent RBCs in the spleen (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) and their local hemolysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) were not rescued by the NAC administration.
claims.evidence: This is supported by heme assay data from NAC-treated mice.

claims.claim: Enhanced RPM lipid peroxidation was not rescued by NAC treatment.
claims.source: Likewise, enhanced RPM lipid peroxidation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), a ferroptosis marker, the formation of insoluble aggregates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), and splenic iron overload (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G) were equally present in aged mice regardless of the NAC treatment.
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from NAC-treated mice.

claims.claim: The formation of insoluble aggregates was not rescued by NAC treatment.
claims.source: Likewise, enhanced RPM lipid peroxidation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), a ferroptosis marker, the formation of insoluble aggregates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), and splenic iron overload (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G) were equally present in aged mice regardless of the NAC treatment.
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological data from NAC-treated mice.

claims.claim: Splenic iron overload was not rescued by NAC treatment.
claims.source: Likewise, enhanced RPM lipid peroxidation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), a ferroptosis marker, the formation of insoluble aggregates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), and splenic iron overload (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G) were equally present in aged mice regardless of the NAC treatment.
claims.evidence: This is supported by iron assay data from NAC-treated mice.

claims.claim: RPM dysfunction and damage during aging are chiefly driven by RPM iron loading rather than excessive ROS.
claims.source: These data suggest that RPM dysfunction and damage during aging are chiefly driven by RPM iron loading rather than excessive ROS.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of rescue by NAC treatment despite successful ROS reduction.

claims.claim: iRPMs significantly decreased the ability for RBC uptake upon iron overload with FAC.
claims.source: We confirmed that iRPMs significantly decreased the ability for RBC uptake upon iron overload with FAC in a manner that was partially rescued by the iron chelator desferrioxamine (DFO; Figure 6A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and confocal microscopy data from in vitro experiments.

claims.claim: The decrease in RBC uptake by iRPMs upon iron overload was partially rescued by the iron chelator DFO.
claims.source: We confirmed that iRPMs significantly decreased the ability for RBC uptake upon iron overload with FAC in a manner that was partially rescued by the iron chelator desferrioxamine (DFO; Figure 6A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and confocal microscopy data from in vitro experiments.

claims.claim: Iron loading by FAC suppressed lysosomal activity in iRPMs.
claims.source: In addition, we observed that iron loading by FAC suppressed lysosomal activity, an important factor for RBC degradation (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro experiments.

claims.claim: Mitochondria membrane potential was similarly diminished by FAC and DFO alone in iRPMs.
claims.source: We also found that mitochondria membrane potential was similarly diminished by FAC and DFO alone, thus uncoupling the phagocytic and lysosomal activity of iRPMs from their mitochondria fitness (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro experiments.

claims.claim: Iron loading reduced protein expression levels of the phosphatidylserine receptors MERTK, AXL, and TIM4 in iRPMs.
claims.source: Mechanistically, we found that iron loading reduced protein expression levels of the receptors that recognize phosphatidylserine on apoptotic cells MERTK, AXL, and TIM4, and which are highly expressed by RPMs (Slusarczyk and Mleczko-Sanecka, 2021), likely contributing to EP (Figure 6E–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro experiments and a citation to literature on RPM receptors.

claims.claim: Expression levels of STAB2 or the Fc receptor CD16 were unchanged upon iron/DFO treatment of iRPMs.
claims.source: Of note, expression levels of another phosphatidylserine receptor STAB2 or the Fc receptor CD16 that as well are present in RPMs (Slusarczyk and Mleczko-Sanecka, 2021) were unchanged upon iron/DFO treatment of iRPMs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro experiments and a citation to literature on RPM receptors.

claims.claim: Iron accumulation reduced calcium levels in iRPMs.
claims.source: Consistent with the important role of calcium signaling in the regulation of EP (Ma et al., 2021), we observed that iron accumulation reduced calcium levels in iRPMs (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro experiments and a citation to literature on calcium signaling in EP.

claims.claim: The effects of iron excess on the levels of apoptotic cell receptors and calcium in iRPMs were rescued by DFO.
claims.source: Importantly, the effects of iron excess on the levels of the apoptotic cell receptors and calcium were rescued by DFO.
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro experiments.
